new_statements.quote: All Folopa words have a pattern of tone and stress. These are not marked on the words because there are very few that would cause confusion to a Folopa reader. [...] In general, the important tone stress is on the last syllable of a basic word. A basic word is one without any added suffixes. When suffixes are added to nouns the tone and stress does not change. It still occurs on the last syllable of the noun. When suffixes are added to verbs the stress and tone moves to the right so that it is on the suffix itself.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has Folopa with an empty rule; this work supplies a placement: 'the important tone stress is on the last syllable of a basic word' (unsuffixed stem), with the domain-of-stress detail that noun suffixes do not shift it while verb suffixes attract it. The work is a pedagogical primer, not a phonology; it conflates tone and stress ('tone stress') and also says Folopa has lexical tone (high/mid/low minimal sets), so the placement statement is about a combined tone-stress prominence, not stress alone. An explicit counter-example on p. 12 ('kale sweet potato (stress on first syllable)') shows the final-syllable rule is 'in general' only.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary prominence (described as combined 'tone stress') falls on the last syllable of the bare (unsuffixed) word. Adding suffixes to a noun leaves prominence on the noun's final syllable; adding suffixes to a verb shifts prominence rightward onto the suffix, i.e. onto the final syllable of the inflected verb. Folopa also has lexical tone: minimal sets yia (high) 'mosquito' / yia (low) 'fish'; boką high/mid/low 'black bird' / 'large bat' / 'dark soil' (p. 8).
new_statements.exceptions: 'In general' hedge; p. 12 glosses kale 'sweet potato' as '(stress on first syllable)'; p. 5 says that in the unique a'a / aa vowel sequence 'the stress of the word is sometimes heard on the second [a] as in the word faalopó, meaning will go'.
new_statements.identity_note: Anderson's materials describe the Folopa spoken in the Fuyuge/Folopa area of Gulf Province, PNG (SIL-PNG programme, ISO ppo); no dialect is named. MacDonald 1973 uses the older name 'Polopa'.

sources.quote: p.129: 'It is suspected that further investigation would reveal the presence of phonemic tone in Polopa. One example is AUR and BOR yá fish vs. ya mosquito.' p.133: 'Tone is common to Daribi, Polopa, Pawaia and Witu, but is not apparent in neighboring groups.' No statement on stress placement (survey wordlist data only).
